results.summary: This design implements a SHA-256 hasher that generates a digest for data of arbitrary length. Data is fed in 64-byte blocks through an 8-bit input port, with control signals for starting, clocking data, and reading the 32-byte result. It requires an external microcontroller to provide data and read results, and supports a parallel mode for interleaving input and processing. The implementation is naive and unoptimized, with estimated throughput of about 6 MB/s at 50 MHz, and a silicon test report indicates it worked in one test run but not a second.

This is a 2-trit balanced ternary ALU that is part of the REBEL-2 balanced ternary logic CPU. It supports operations such as MIN, MAX, ADD, SUB, MUL, CMP, and SHFT, which can be performed trit-wise or word-wise. The design is generated and verified using the Mixed Radix Circuit Synthesizer (MRCS), and while automated tests exist for MRCS, a Verilog testbench and FPGA constraint file are still work in progress. The documentation is limited and the project appears to be a work in progress.

This project is titled Reflex Game and is intended to be a reflex-based game using a 7-segment display. However, the documentation states that it does not work and suggests making a testbench. There is no description of how the game operates or how it is tested. The design is essentially undocumented and non-functional.

This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square wave tone generators, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with 10 shapes. It is controlled via an 8-bit multiplexed data/address bus and produces audio through either an 8-bit digital output for an external DAC or a PWM output for analog filtering. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to hear the audio. Silicon test reports indicate it works well, with users successfully playing chiptunes and using the 128 divider mode.

This design implements a cellular automaton based on Rule 110, executing over 200 cells in parallel every clock cycle. It includes a parallel read/write bus for accessing and modifying cell states in 8-cell blocks, with control pins for halt and write enable. The automaton can be used for exploring complex behavior, pseudo-random number generation, and data compression, and is known to be Turing complete. The design is well-documented with timing diagrams and examples, and no external hardware is required beyond a clock and control signals.

This is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square wave tone generators and one noise generator with white and periodic noise. It is programmed via an 8-bit data bus and provides both digital 8-bit audio output and PWM output for analog audio. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to produce sound. The design is well-documented, includes a test suite, and aims for hardware preservation and education.

This project implements a 3-layer spiking neural network with on-chip weights. It has an 8-bit input bus, control signals for execution and synchronization, and outputs from the last layer's neurons. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it is a 3-layer spiking neural net with on-chip weights and that testing begins after reset. There is insufficient information to describe its operation, external hardware requirements, or notable features.

This design is a Field Programmable Neural Array (FPNA) consisting of 50 interconnected configurable neuron blocks (CNBs) that simulate leaky neurons. Each CNB has four inputs with 3-bit weights, a configurable decay rate, and fires when its membrane potential reaches a threshold, sending pulses to neighboring neurons. Configuration is done via a bitstream shifted in through dedicated pins, and the network can be trained using the accompanying naxon tool. The design is intended for neuromorphic computing research and requires external clocking and configuration data to operate.

This design uses three rotary encoders to control three PWM generators, likely for RGB LED mixing. It includes debouncing for the encoder inputs and provides debug outputs for the encoder values and debounce signals. The encoders are connected to the first six input pins, and the PWM outputs appear on the first three output pins. A silicon test report from the author confirms all three channels work up to 50 MHz.

This is a basic calculator chip that implements an 8-bit ALU with operations including add, subtract, bitwise logic, shifts, and comparisons. It uses input pins for the number and operation selection, an enter pin to latch commands, and output pins for the result and flags (overflow, negative, zero). The design is controlled by a clock and reset, and is intended to be tested by entering numbers and operations. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand its function.
